newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn says exports remain pillar of growth.
newsitem.headline: Bonn says exports remain pillar of growth.

text.p: Exports remained the most important pillar of the German economy in the third quarter, but growth was also fuelled by government spending and health care, the Economics Ministry said Friday.
"Exports of goods and services grew strongly, while imports increased only slightly," the ministry said in its December monthly report.
"As in the first half, state consumption made a significant contribution to growth. This was led by an unexpectedly strong increase in outlays by health care bodies."
Such costs rose as the government disability insurance scheme included in-patient care for the first time, it said.
As reported earlier, the German economy grew 1 percent in the third quarter from the previous quarter and 2.4 percent from the year-ago quarter, according to ministry data.
The year-on-year growth rate was up from 1.2 percent in the second quarter and 0.2 percent in the first quarter.

The construction sector remained weak in the third quarter, but investment increased slightly, boosted by the acceleration of some projects in east Germany to take advantage of a tax break that ends this year.
"Excluding such special factors, the basic tendency in construction investment may still have been downward," the report said.
Private consumption showed no growth as real incomes stagnated, while capital investment was also flat.
The labour market continued to deteriorate. "An improvement in the employment situation is generally delayed by several quarters from the start of an economic recovery," it said.
But the recovery remained slow-paced, and lacked breadth. "Domestic investment, the most important pace-setter for growth and employment, remains sluggish."
Companies remain reluctant to invest because important policy questions are in debate, including tax reform and the financially viable transformation of the social safety net.
Germany's trade surplus in the first nine months of 1996 totalled 69.1 billion marks ($44.8 billion). Exports increased 3.6 percent while imports grew only 2.4 percent.
Its current account, which includes trade in services, was in deficit by 44.6 billion marks ($28.9 billion) that was 1.1 billion marks ($712.4 million) less than in the year-earlier period.
